title: Range hood: safe teardown
summary: A kitchen range hood gives a small mains blower motor with its fan or blower wheel, washable aluminium grease filters, lamp holders and bulbs, switches and a stainless or painted steel shell. Many are wired straight into the house circuit, so switch off the breaker and prove the wires dead before touching them. The shell has sharp edges and the insides are coated in grease that burns.

steps.text: Check what it is. If the "hood" is a microwave oven mounted over the cooker, stop and use teardown_microwave instead. If it is a restaurant hood with a fire suppression tank, pipes and nozzles, leave that system alone and see the notes.
steps.warn: An over-the-range microwave holds a high-voltage capacitor that can kill even when unplugged.

steps.text: Isolate it. First list every source that could feed it: the grid, a generator, a solar or battery inverter, a UPS. Switch off any inverter and its DC isolator as well as the grid, because solar and battery systems can keep a house live with the grid dead. Some hoods plug into an outlet inside the cabinet above: unplug it and keep the plug where you can see it. Others are wired into the house circuit through a box on the hood: switch off the breaker that feeds it and lock or tag it (see safety_mains_isolation). The hood's own switches are not isolation.

Set up before you open anything. Cooker off and cold. Lay a board or thick card over the cooktop. Stand a stepladder on firm, level floor beside the cooker, never on the cooktop or the counter edge, with a helper footing it; near wiring use a wooden or fibreglass ladder if you have one, not a metal one. Put on leather or cut-resistant gloves and safety glasses: hood edges, filter frames and the blower housing cut deeply. Keep your meter and tools in a pouch, not in your hands, keep three points of contact on the ladder, never lean sideways, and don't work alone or in the dark.
Slide or unlatch the grease filters from the underside and bag them.
steps.warn: Filters and the inside of the hood are coated in grease that burns. Keep grinders, torches and flames away until it is cleaned.

steps.text: Take out the bulbs and their lens covers. Hold each bulb by its glass and keep fingers out of the socket until the wires have been proved dead.
steps.warn: A lamp that was on recently can still be hot.

steps.text: Open the wiring box cover on the hood without touching the bare wires. Set the meter to AC volts (600 V or higher, or auto) with the leads in the COM and V sockets, and prove it on a known live source such as a working socket or a generator outlet. Then test live to neutral, live to earth and neutral to earth at the house wires. Then prove the meter on the live source again: if it doesn't read now, your test proved nothing. Don't trust a non-contact voltage pen on its own.
steps.warn: If anything reads live, stop. Find and switch off the right breaker before going on.

steps.text: Undo the connectors joining the hood's wires to the house wires. Cap each house wire on its own with a connector or tape, and fold them back into the cabinet or wall box so the circuit is left safe. Leave the breaker off and tagged until you have finished.

With a helper taking the weight of the hood from below, loosen its mounting screws (often four, into the cabinet bottom or the wall), take out the last one, and lower the hood, sliding it off the duct connector. On keyhole mountings, lift the hood slightly and slide it off the screw heads.
steps.warn: A typical hood weighs about 10 kg or more and is awkward overhead. The helper on the floor takes the weight before the last screw comes out; never carry it down the ladder. Don't stand on the cooktop or counter edge: glass cooktops break.

steps.text: On the bench, wipe off the worst grease with hot soapy water or a degreaser. Then open the blower housing or motor cover (screws or clips).

If there is a capacitor beside the motor (a small can or block with two terminals; some blower motors have one), deal with it first. Make sure at least 5 minutes have passed since the circuit was isolated, drain the capacitor through your resistor tool, then measure DC volts across its terminals and from each terminal to the frame until it reads near zero (see safety_discharge_capacitor). Only then unplug the motor's connector, undo the screws or nuts that hold the motor, and lift it out with its fan blade or blower wheel.
Take the switches or the push-button board, and the light sockets with a length of wire on each.
Keep a carbon filter only if it is new and still sealed. A used one is spent.
Strip the shell for sheet steel. Unscrew the panels you want and fold or file any cut edge.
steps.warn: Hood edges can be very sharp. Wear gloves and eye protection.

steps.text: Take the metal duct and the backdraft damper if you need them.
steps.warn: Duct may be galvanised (a dull grey zinc coating with a crystal pattern). Never use galvanised metal for a stove pipe or weld it: heated zinc gives off toxic fumes.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Blower motor and fan.** A small mains motor. The Cosmo 5MU30 motor takes 125 W at 110–120 V (Cosmo 5MU guide); the whole Broan 41000 hood draws 2.0 A at 120 V, and its motor runs at no more than 2,850 rpm (Broan 41000 spec). Broan motors are permanently lubricated with sealed bearings; after three years of heavy use a few drops of oil on each bearing help (Broan 43000 guide). Use it as a kitchen, workshop or latrine extractor, a dehydrator fan or a smoke fan wherever mains power exists. Run it on its own speed switch: Broan says not to use these hoods with a solid-state speed control (Broan 43000 guide).
- **Grease filters.** Aluminium mesh panels. Broan's can go in a dishwasher (Broan 43000 guide); Cosmo's are hand-wash only (Cosmo 5MU guide). Clean, they make a coarse washable pre-filter for a fan intake or a drying tray.
- **Carbon filter.** Ductless hoods use a charcoal filter or pad. Broan says a saturated one can't be reactivated (Broan 43000 guide), and Cosmo's can't be washed (Cosmo 5MU guide). Only a new, sealed spare is worth taking; use it for odour filtering in air, not for drinking water.
- **Lights.** Broan's 43000 takes an E26 LED bulb of up to 15 W (Broan 43000 guide). The Cosmo 5MU30 has 3 W back LEDs (Cosmo 5MU30 spec) and E26 bulbs of up to 40 W (Cosmo 5MU guide). Bulbs and sockets are spares for any mains lighting.
- **Switches.** Rocker switches for fan and light (Broan 41000 spec) or a push-button control board (Cosmo 5MU guide).
- **Power cord.** Plug-in hoods like the Cosmo 5MU30 come with a 3-prong cord (Cosmo 5MU30 spec).
- **The shell.** The Cosmo 5MU30 is 430-grade stainless steel (Cosmo 5MU30 spec); Broan sells painted and stainless versions with hemmed bottom edges (Broan 41000 spec). Flat stainless sheet makes a heat shield behind a stove, a splash panel or a reflector.
- **Duct and damper.** Broan says to use only metal duct (Broan 43000 guide). Plain steel duct is useful pipe; galvanised duct must stay away from fire (build_rocket_stove).

## Testing what you got out

- **Motor:** it should spin freely by hand with no grinding. Check its windings with the meter, and from each lead to the frame (test_motor). If you then run it, clamp it down, use a fused supply with the terminals covered, discharge any capacitor first, and keep hands, hair and loose clothing well clear of the blade: Cosmo warns that blowers catch hair, fingers and loose clothing (Cosmo 5MU guide).
- **Switches and sockets:** check them for continuity (test_continuity).

## Variations

- **Under-cabinet hoods:** the Broan 43000 hangs on four screws under the cabinet (Broan 43000 guide); the Cosmo 5MU30 uses four screws under the cabinet or four in the wall (Cosmo 5MU guide).
- **Ducted or ductless.** The Broan 41000 is a non-ducted hood (Broan 41000 spec); the 43000 can be ducted or run non-ducted with a charcoal filter (Broan 43000 guide).
- **Plug-in or hard-wired.** The Broan 43000 is wired into a box on the hood unless an approved cord kit is fitted (Broan 43000 guide); the Cosmo 5MU30 plugs in (Cosmo 5MU30 spec). For a hard-wired hood, use a ladder with nonconductive side rails if there is any chance of touching live wiring (OSHA ladders).
- **Restaurant hoods** may carry a wet-chemical fire suppression system. The Ansul R-102 uses a gas cartridge to drive agent from tanks at 110 psi (7.6 bar) working pressure, is set off automatically when heat-sensitive fusible links separate, and can be fitted to shut off gas and power to the cooking line (Ansul R-102 data sheet). If the agent gets in your eyes or on your skin, flush it with water (Ansulex data sheet).

## What to leave

- The fire suppression tanks, cartridges, links and pipework on a restaurant hood. The system is built to fire on its own.
- Plastic blades and covers that are cracked or soaked with grease.
- Grease-soaked insulation or foam.
- A used carbon filter.
